---
title: "The exponential family"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Many GLM response distributions share the **exponential-family form**. The point of this notation is computational: once the density is written this way, derivatives of the same function $b(\theta)$ supply the mean and variance used by the score and Hessian. Recall that a [PMF](../random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd) assigns mass to possible discrete response values, whereas the [expectation of a function](../random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions.qmd) averages that function under the distribution. A discrete member can be written in the form stated below.

We first identify the shared algebraic pieces, then recover the mean and variance, and finally map the Bernoulli, Poisson, and Gaussian families into that template.

$$
p(y\mid\theta,\phi)=\exp\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}.
$$

For an absolutely continuous member, the same form is written as a PDF (f(y\mid\theta,\phi)). We use (p) only for the discrete Bernoulli member below.

Here $\theta$ is the canonical parameter, $b(\theta)$ determines the mean and variance, $a(\phi)$ scales dispersion, and $c(y,\phi)$ supplies the base measure needed to make the mass or density integrate to one. To derive the moment identities, start from that normalizing requirement:

$$
1=\int \exp\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}\,d\nu(y).
$$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $\theta$ and move the derivative inside the integral. The left side is zero, so

$$
0=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Y-b'(\theta)}{a(\phi)}\right],
\qquad\text{and thus}\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y]=b'(\theta).
$$

Differentiating again, or differentiating $\mathbb{E}[Y]$, gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y]=a(\phi)b''(\theta).
$$

These steps assume differentiation and integration may be interchanged. To make the roles concrete, we now derive the Bernoulli member from the observed SuperTelicity choices.

```{r}
#| label: observed-bernoulli-mass
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
counts <- as.data.frame(table(st$preposition))
names(counts) <- c("preposition", "observations")
counts$probability <- counts$observations / sum(counts$observations)
counts
```

For $y_i\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
p(y_i\mid\pi_i)=\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}.
$$

Set $\theta_i=\log[\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)]$. Because $\pi_i=e^{\theta_i}/(1+e^{\theta_i})$,

$$
\log p(y_i\mid\theta_i)=y_i\theta_i-\log(1+e^{\theta_i}).
$$

Thus $b(\theta)=\log(1+e^\theta)$ and $a(\phi)=1$. Differentiating $b$ recovers $b'(\theta)=\pi$ and $b''(\theta)=\pi(1-\pi)$.

| Family | $\theta$ | $b(\theta)$ | $a(\phi)$ | Mean | Variance |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Bernoulli | $\log[\pi/(1-\pi)]$ | $\log(1+e^\theta)$ | $1$ | $\pi$ | $\pi(1-\pi)$ |
| Poisson | $\log\lambda$ | $e^\theta$ | $1$ | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ |
| Normal with known variance $\sigma^2$ | $\mu$ | $\theta^2/2$ | $\sigma^2$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma^2$ |

```{r}
#| label: observed-bernoulli-likelihood
#| echo: true
y <- st$prep_in
pi_hat <- mean(y)
log_likelihood <- sum(dbinom(y, size = 1L, prob = pi_hat, log = TRUE))
c(rows = length(y), in_responses = sum(y), probability_in = pi_hat,
  log_likelihood = log_likelihood,
  bernoulli_variance = pi_hat * (1 - pi_hat))
```

The shared form links distributions to GLM computation, but it does not make the families interchangeable. Bernoulli, Poisson, and normal models retain different supports and mean–variance relations. The exponential-family notation organizes those distinctions; it does not remove them.

## Recap and check

1. Does membership in the exponential family allow a Poisson model for binary data? No. Family membership does not erase support or variance restrictions.
2. What work does $c(y,\phi)$ do? It contains response-dependent terms, including the base measure, required for normalization even when those terms do not contain $\theta$.

The [sufficient-statistics page](sufficient-statistics.qmd) uses the same factorized likelihood to ask exactly which sample features retain information about a parameter.
